notes.meaning: Moses spent forty years working quietly as a shepherd in the desert for his father-in-law. He guided the flock to Mount Horeb, which is another name for Mount Sinai where God would later give the Law. God often prepares his servants through humble daily work before giving them great tasks.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars believe the text was woven together from different ancient documents, such as the J, E, and P sources, which should not be forced into one timeline.

notes.meaning: The Lord appeared to Moses in a blazing fire inside a desert thornbush. Moses saw that the bush was flaming with fire, yet the branches did not burn up. This showed God's holy presence among his suffering people, protecting them from being destroyed by their trials.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: Both traditions see the unburned bush as a picture of Mary, who gave birth to Christ while remaining a virgin.

notes.meaning: Moses was amazed by what he saw and walked closer to get a better look. He wanted to understand why a common thornbush could be on fire without turning to ash. God used this wondrous sight to draw Moses' attention so he could speak to him.

When the Lord saw Moses turn aside to look, he called out to him by name from within the bush. Repeating his name showed urgent love and personal care. Moses answered right away, showing that he was ready to listen and obey.

God told Moses not to come any closer and ordered him to take off his sandals. The ground had become holy because the holy God was present there. Taking off sandals showed deep respect, humility, and reverence before God's majesty.

God announced that he is the same God who made a covenant—a binding sacred promise—with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Hearing this, Moses covered his face because he felt reverent awe and knew that humans cannot look directly at God. This reminded Moses that God remembers and keeps his promises to his people across generations.

The Lord told Moses that he had closely watched the misery of the Israelites in Egypt. He heard their desperate cries under their cruel slave drivers and knew all their pain. God is never blind to the troubles of his people when they suffer.

God promised to come down and rescue Israel from the power of the Egyptians. He planned to lead them to Canaan, a wide and fruitful land described as flowing with milk and honey. Deliverance was not just about freeing them from slavery, but bringing them into a rich home of their own.

God repeated that the cries of the Israelites had reached him in heaven. He had witnessed the harsh cruelty and injustice the Egyptians inflicted on them every day. The time had now arrived for God to step in and act on their behalf.

God gave Moses his marching orders, sending him back to Pharaoh the king of Egypt. Moses was to lead the entire nation of Israel out of slavery. Although God alone had the power to save them, he chose to work through a human leader.

Moses felt completely inadequate for such an enormous mission and asked, 'Who am I?' Forty years earlier he had been confident, but time as a shepherd taught him his own weakness before kings. God often calls people when they recognize they have no strength of their own.

God answered Moses' fear by promising to be personally present with him every step of the way. He gave Moses a sign: after leading the people out of Egypt, they would all return to worship God at this very mountain. True confidence comes not from our own ability, but from God's promise to stay with us.

Moses asked God what name he should tell the Israelites if they questioned who sent him. In Egypt, people worshipped many false gods who all had individual names. Moses wanted to give the people a clear name that revealed who the true God was and proved his authority.

God answered Moses by declaring his name as 'I AM WHO I AM,' telling him to say that 'I AM' had sent him. This name means God is self-existent, having life completely in himself without depending on anyone or anything else. He is also eternal, unchanging, and entirely faithful to carry out all his promises.

differ.view: Some Reformed teachers emphasize that the name primarily promises God's active, saving presence with His people rather than just defining His abstract eternal being.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars see the name as expressing God's ongoing, active presence with his people throughout history rather than only an abstract statement about his eternal being.

notes.meaning: God told Moses to identify him to Israel as the Lord, the God of their ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. This personal name, Yahweh, is God's memorial name to be remembered in every generation. It assured the Israelites that the God making promises now is the same faithful God who watched over their fathers.

God instructed Moses to gather the elders, who were the respected heads and leaders of the Israelite families. He was to tell them that the God of their fathers had appeared to him with a message of hope. God had closely examined their harsh treatment and was actively stepping in to help them.

God gave a firm promise to lead the people up out of their suffering in Egypt. He pledged to bring them into the fertile and productive land occupied by the Canaanite nations. God's purpose was sure, giving the weary slaves confidence that their freedom was at hand.

God assured Moses that the elders of Israel would listen to his words and believe him. Then Moses and the elders were to go together to Pharaoh and ask permission to take a three-day journey into the wilderness to offer sacrifices to the Lord. God intended to lead his people out into the desert so they could worship him freely away from Egyptian idolatry.

God warned Moses in advance that the king of Egypt would stubbornly refuse their request. Pharaoh would not let the people leave until God compelled him with immense power. Knowing this beforehand prepared Moses so he would not lose heart when Pharaoh resisted.

God declared that he would stretch out his hand and strike Egypt with miraculous signs and plagues. These displays of divine power would punish the oppressors and show God's supremacy over Egypt's rulers. Only after experiencing these wonders would Pharaoh finally let Israel go.

God promised to make the Egyptians look favorably upon the Israelites before they left. When the time came for their departure, the people would not leave empty-handed after centuries of unpaid labor. God has ways of moving the hearts of even harsh enemies to show kindness to his people.

Israelite women were directed to ask their Egyptian neighbors for silver, gold, and fine clothing to put on their children. This was not stealing or deceitful borrowing, but receiving rightful payment and plunder from a defeated oppressor. God ensured his people received fair recompense for their long years of hard slave labor.
